analysis.one_liner: Taxes fund managers' performance pay as ordinary income instead of at lower capital gains rates.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Ways and Means Committee without a vote, with no cosponsors in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: Fund managers at private equity and hedge funds are typically paid a share of their funds' profits, called carried interest. The tax code taxes those profits at the lower capital gains rate — around 20% for high earners — rather than as ordinary income at up to 37%. This bill would change that, taxing managers' performance pay like a salary, ending related breaks on selling their fund stakes, and adding a penalty for tax-avoidance schemes. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in two ways: investment fund managers' pay would be taxed at the same rates as a worker's paycheck, and the added revenue would come from some of the highest-earning people in the country, easing the burden on everyone else or funding public priorities. Wage earners effectively subsidize this break today, since salary income is taxed at rates up to 37% while carried interest gets the roughly 20% capital gains rate.

how_it_helps.text: It taxes carried interest — the share of fund profits paid to investment managers — as ordinary income instead of at the lower long-term capital gains rate, which can nearly double the tax rate on that income.

It closes related routes around the rule: gains on selling the manager's stake are taxed as ordinary income, dividends and small-business stock breaks are denied on that income, the payments are counted as self-employment income subject to Medicare and Social Security taxes, and a 40 percent penalty applies to underpayments from avoiding the rules.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital fund managers, whose profit-based pay would be taxed at ordinary income rates instead of lower capital gains rates, and who would face payroll taxes and a 40% penalty for avoidance schemes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: The change would significantly raise taxes on investment fund managers, who argue the current lower rates compensate for the risky, performance-based nature of their pay and help attract capital management talent.

The rules are complicated — they rely on the Treasury to write anti-abuse regulations and include carve-outs for family partnerships and real estate trusts, which could create loopholes or compliance costs even for honest taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is that fund managers would pay the same tax rates on their labor income as everyone else, raising revenue without touching most households. The drawbacks are that some investment managers would face meaningful tax increases, defenders of the current rules argue the preferential rate encourages long-term investment and risk-taking, and the bill's complexity would invite planning and enforcement battles. The main limitation, though, is that it never moved at all, so none of these effects were ever tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and died there when the congressional session ended, with no cosponsors and no vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on October 11, 2024, less than a month before the 118th Congress ended, and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee.
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers keep the carried interest tax break, which lets their performance-based pay be taxed at lower capital gains rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end the carried interest tax treatment.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after it was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.what_they_did: Has long lobbied against carried interest tax increases, contributing to why such provisions have repeatedly failed to become law.

sides.party_line_note: No votes occurred; the sponsor was a Democrat with zero cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital managers
industries.note: Their main form of pay — carried interest — would be taxed as ordinary income at higher rates and subject to payroll taxes, plus a new 40 percent avoidance penalty. Their interest runs against the public's here: the current break saves them billions while their labor income is taxed more lightly than a nurse's paycheck.

Partnerships receiving investment management services face new ordinary-income treatment, valuation, and reporting rules on service-partner interests, though genuine capital contributions from non-service investors remain protected.
